info.name: Adwa Admin API (Developer 1)
info.description:
End-to-end functional and tenant-isolation tests for the Developer 1 admin surface.

Run the folders **in order, from the top**: later requests depend on tokens and IDs that earlier ones save. The collection is designed to be run repeatedly — every resource it creates is named with a per-run unique suffix and is deleted again in `06 Cleanup`.

Two checks run automatically on **every** request via the collection-level test script:

- every response carries an `X-Request-Id` header (§7.4)
- every response of 400 or above uses the §7.1 error envelope (`error.message`, `error.code`, `error.requestId`)

See `postman/README.md` for setup, the rate-limit caveat, and the regression guards it carries.

item.name: 01 Auth
item.description:
Logs in the two seeded accounts and saves their tokens, then works through the failure modes: indistinguishable credential errors, missing and malformed tokens, and malformed or oversized request bodies.

**Rate limit note:** `POST /admin/login` is capped at 10 requests per IP per 15 minutes outside `NODE_ENV=test`. This collection spends 5 of those per run, so two back-to-back runs fit and a third will legitimately return `429 RATE_LIMITED`. Restart `npm run dev` to reset the in-memory window.

item.name: 03 Rooms
item.description:
Room CRUD plus the two rules that make the tour sequence trustworthy: `nextRoomId` must point inside the same museum, and it must never form a cycle.

The first two requests are the important ones — they send a *different* museum's id in the body and query string and prove the server ignores both in favour of the token.

Creates `roomA` (kept for folders 04-05), a delete-flow pair, and `roomB` inside museum B.

request.description: **The single most important request in the collection.** The body explicitly asks for museum B, and the museum admin's token says museum A. If the server ever honoured the body, one museum could write content into another's tour. The assertion checks the created room landed in A.

item.name: 05 Tenant isolation
item.description:
The live-server mirror of the automated isolation matrix. Every request here uses **museum A's token against museum B's resources** and must be refused, then the same request as the system admin must succeed — proving the refusals come from scope enforcement and not from a broken route.

The distinction that matters: `CROSS_TENANT_ACCESS` means "this resource exists and is not yours"; `FORBIDDEN` means "this action is not available to your role at all".

exec: pm.test('No museum data leaked in the error body', function () {

request.description: Matrix case: museum admin reads another museum.
Matrix case: museum admin reads another museum's room.
Matrix case: museum admin edits another museum's room. Scope is checked before the body is validated, so a well-formed malicious edit is refused just as firmly as a malformed one.
Matrix case: museum admin deletes another museum's room — with `force=true`, the most destructive form. Refused before the force flag is even read.

Matrix case: items are listed by `roomId`, which is a query field. Scope therefore cannot be checked by middleware — it is checked in the service after the room is loaded from the database, and this proves that check is really there.

item.name: A -> B items: POST into B's room (403)

request.description: Matrix case: the write-side version of the previous request. `roomId` arrives in the body, so this is the path an attacker would actually try.
Matrix case: an item has no `museumId` column. Its tenant is resolved by joining through its room, and this proves that join is what gates access.
Matrix case: museum admin deletes another museum's item.
Matrix case: the reorder route lives under `/rooms` but is implemented in the items module. Easy to forget when adding scope checks, so it gets its own probe.

exec: pm.test('403 FORBIDDEN — role gate, not a scope error', function () {

request.description: Matrix case: museum A editing **its own** museum, which it is otherwise allowed to do — but `status` is reserved for the platform operator. Otherwise a suspended museum could simply un-suspend itself. The code is `FORBIDDEN` because this is a field-level role rule, not a tenant boundary.

exec: pm.test('200 OK — the system admin crosses tenants by design', function () {
pm.test('It really is museum B\'s room', function () {

request.description: **The control case.** Every 403 above must be caused by scope enforcement, not by a route that is simply broken or a resource that does not exist. The same request with a system-admin token returns 200, which proves the resource is reachable and the refusals were deliberate.
Suspension is the supported way to cut a museum off — there is deliberately no museum delete, so a non-paying tenant's content is preserved rather than destroyed.

**Matrix case worth reading closely.** This token was issued *before* the suspension and is still cryptographically valid for hours. Access is refused anyway, because `requireAuth` re-reads the museum's status from the database on every single request. Without that, suspending a museum would do nothing until its admins' tokens happened to expire.
Suspension is reversible and does not touch content.

item.name: 06 Cleanup
item.description:
Removes everything this run created, so the collection can be run again immediately against the same database.

The one thing that cannot be cleaned up is museum B itself: there is deliberately no museum delete route (suspension replaces it). It is left SUSPENDED so leftover QA tenants are visibly inert. Deleting them, if they pile up, is a database job — see the README.

request.description: Deleting a room cascades to its items at the database level, so the museum B item goes with it.
